opus-5.5.text:
That's a distinction we spend a lot of time on, because people often treat them as the same thing, and they're really not.

When you test the model itself, you're trying to understand its raw capabilities and risks: what it can do, where it fails, and what harmful content it might produce in the wrong hands. That's very open-ended. You probe across a huge range of scenarios, because the model could end up in almost any context. You're asking questions like: Can it be jailbroken easily? Does it produce dangerous information? How does it handle sensitive topics? That work feeds into model-level mitigations like safety training. It also tells us what we need to communicate to the people building on top of it.

Testing an application is much more grounded. Once you know the use case, say a customer service bot, a coding assistant, or a tool that summarizes medical records, you can define what "good" and "bad" look like far more precisely. The risks shift. A model can be perfectly safe in general and still fail badly in your application. It might hallucinate facts about your product, leak information from your retrieval system, or be manipulated through a prompt injection hidden in a document it's reading. None of that shows up in model-level testing, because it comes from the whole system: the metaprompt, the data sources, the tools it can call, the user interface, and the people actually using it.

So we think of it as layers. The model layer gives you a foundation. Then at the application layer you add things like safety system messages, content filters, grounding, and user experience design. You have to test that full stack together, in the context of real usage. And it's not a one-time thing. You red team to discover risks you hadn't anticipated. Then you turn those findings into systematic measurements you can run repeatedly as you iterate. Then you keep monitoring once it's in production, because users will always find things you didn't think of.

The short version is that model testing tells you what's possible, and application testing tells you what actually happens. You need both.

r001.rationale: It describes probing what harmful content the model could produce “in the wrong hands,” including jailbreaks and dangerous information.

r002.rationale: It discusses model capabilities and risks but does not describe testing whether the model behaves appropriately out of the box when used as intended.

r003.rationale: It says application testing is grounded in a defined use case, allowing more precise criteria for good and bad outcomes.

r004.rationale: It calls for testing the full application stack and repeated measurements, but does not describe scoring outcomes across a sequence of interactions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is a distinction we spend a lot of time on, because I think people conflate the two constantly, and they're really different problems.

When you're testing the model, you're asking a very broad question: what is this thing capable of, across basically every input someone could throw at it? So you're probing for the full surface area. Can it produce harmful content, does it hallucinate, how does it handle different languages, how does it respond to jailbreaks. It's foundational work, and it's intentionally context-free, because the model is going to get used in a thousand different ways you can't predict. The output of that testing is more like a capability and risk profile than a pass/fail.

Testing an application is a completely different exercise, because now you have context. You know who the users are, you know what they're trying to do, you know what the system prompt says, what data is being retrieved, what tools the model can call, what the UI shows. All of that changes the risk picture. A model that's a little too willing to write persuasive text might be totally fine in a marketing copy assistant and a real problem in a customer-facing chatbot for a bank. So application testing is grounded in scenarios. You're asking, for my users, in my domain, with my mitigations in place, what actually happens?

And the thing I'd emphasize is that the application layer is where most of the real behavior gets determined. The retrieval system, the grounding, the content filters, the prompt, the way you've constrained the task, those are often doing more to shape the experience than the base model is. So you can't just inherit the model's test results and call it done. We've seen teams assume that because the model was evaluated by the provider, their product is covered, and that's just not true. The model evaluation tells you about the raw ingredients. It doesn't tell you anything about the dish.

The other practical difference is that application testing has to be iterative and ongoing. You ship a mitigation, you change the prompt, you add a new data source, and the behavior shifts, sometimes in ways that aren't obvious. So you need measurement that lives in your development loop, not a one-time red team before launch. We think about it as: red team early to discover what can go wrong, then build evaluations that let you measure it repeatedly, then put monitoring in production because the real world will always find things your tests didn't.

So the short version is: model testing asks what could this do, application testing asks what will this do here, for these people, with everything I've built around it. You need both, but if you're building a product, the second one is the one you own.

r001.rationale: It mentions harmful content and jailbreaks while describing broad model testing, but does not frame dangerous-capability testing as assessing the worst the model could do if misused.

r002.rationale: It does not describe alignment testing or whether the model behaves appropriately out of the box when used as intended.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes application testing as grounded in the specific users, domain, prompts, retrieved data, tools, and mitigations.

r004.rationale: It discusses scenario-based and ongoing application evaluations, but does not describe scoring the outcome of a sequence of system interactions.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is what you can know at each level. When you’re testing a model, you’re looking broadly at its capabilities and limitations: What kinds of tasks can it do? Where does it fail? Can you get it to generate harmful content? That testing has to cover a wide range of potential uses, because you don’t yet know exactly what application someone will build.

With an application, you have a much more specific context. Who is using it? What are they trying to accomplish? What data does the model have access to, and what actions can it take? You’re testing the whole system—the model, the instructions, the retrieval, the safeguards—and whether that combination works for the intended use.

For example, a model might produce an inaccurate answer, but the implications are very different if it’s helping you brainstorm a party theme versus answering a question that informs a consequential decision. So model testing gives you an important foundation, but it doesn’t replace application testing. You need to evaluate the actual experience and the failures that matter in that context.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of those as two different layers. When you’re testing a model, you’re trying to understand its capabilities and limitations across a broad range of scenarios. What kinds of requests can it handle? Where does it produce incorrect information or harmful content? That gives you a baseline, but it doesn’t tell you whether a particular application is ready to ship.

For the application, you need to test the whole system in the context where people will actually use it. That includes your instructions, any data you retrieve, the tools the model can call, and the safeguards you put around it. A model might perform well on a general benchmark and still fail on something that’s really important for your use case.

So you need application-specific evaluations: representative user interactions, adversarial cases, and clear criteria for what success and failure look like. And then you continue monitoring after deployment, because people will use the application in ways you didn’t anticipate.
